articles.title: Show HN: Kapso – Iterative learning from enterprise data
articles.summary:
Hey HN! We're Alireza and Majid building Leeroo (https://leeroo.com/). Previously we’ve built AI systems for products with millions of users, including at LinkedIn and Meta. We’re now focusing on building AI systems for enterprise data. Today, we're open-sourcing Kapso (https://github.com/Leeroo-AI/kapso), an engine that runs experiments, deploys the best solution, and learns from every run.
The nature of data work is iterative: investigate, form hypotheses, experiment, and improve based on what you learn. This bottom-up process is the only way to deliver meaningful outcomes quickly in large, messy enterprise data environments. Consultants gathering context in meetings or teams defining a business ontology upfront to fit into the data has no chance of execution, in quarters and sometimes years. An AI-native system should automate this process, compounding learning to each new investigation and implementation.
For instance, one of our enterprise projects was moving a company off its old data estate onto a lakehouse with more than 30 source-system families, thousands of tables and transformations, and hundreds of BI reports. No individual or AI agent knew how that data estate was connected and operated. The only way to learn it was to investigate the company's repos, dbt models, documentation, and data itself and propose hypotheses about the estate, run experiments, and learn from them, until we understand how each system behaves and under which conditions.
The iterative work goes beyond understanding how data and systems fit together, and the business operations. Building useful software is iterative too. Whether you’re optimizing a warehouse, building a lakehouse pipeline or predicting churn, you need to run experiments and learn what works best in that environment. As you deliver more projects, that know-how compounds, similar in principle to RL. RAGing documentation has little value until it has been tried in a specific environment and the consequences are learned. As with human engineering work, experimentation and learning should happen in a sandbox.
We built Kapso for this kind of work, you give it an objective and success criteria, and it works towards an optimum solution that can be deployed on your stack.
You can view a video walkthrough here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W4FHlza1fRs
Here’s how it works…
Kapso has a bank of lessons that are induced or deduced from the past experiments, and each carries a credence score, conditions on where it applies, and the evidence behind it.  For each new experiment, an ideation module proposes ideas considering the earlier lessons, re-ranks them by expected return against the budget each would use, and sends the top-ranked ones to the implementor. Because the bank keeps learning from the past experiments in that environment, the proposed ideas are better suited to it than generic hypotheses from an LLM or RAG. Also, results of each experiment are verified by a verifier module that no experiment can access and cheat. As we’ve found when building such systems, sometimes the success criteria and evaluation tests need to be evolved. The experimentation modules can propose updates to the metrics and criteria for the verifier to approve or reject.
After each run, learn() updates the bank of lessons’ scores and boundaries using the evidence from that run. Changes to the bank can also be A/B tested by running otherwise identical builds with the previous and updated banks. The bank is built on git, so you can share your experience with others, list the banks available to you, and update them (`kapso experience share/list/update` in CLI). The system is model-agnostic and coding-agent-agnostic.
kapso.deploy(solution, target_stack) follows the same workflow, runs a shorter experimentation loop to adapt the best solution to the target stack (e.g. Docker, Modal, BentoCloud, LangGraph). Every domain has a harness to start from, you can write your own domain harness with /kapso:harness in the plugin or through CLI (kapso harness new ), and compound over that by running experimentations.
We ran it on some public benchmarks and live competitions, with the following results…
- Predictive modelling on relational databases: first on RelBench, Kumo AI (now Nvidia) and Stanford's benchmark, ahead of the best tabular foundation model (https://star-project.stanford.edu/relbench/leaderboard/). This shows that keeping the learning in the harness-level can beat foundational table models. Updating a bank of lessons costs far less than retraining a tabular foundation model.
- ML Engineering: First on OpenAI's MLE-bench at submission, still among the top open-source systems (https://github.com/openai/mle-bench/pull/107).
- AI competitions: ahead of the best agent the ALE-Bench authors at Sakana AI reported, and running autonomously at the live International Olympiad in AI 2026, above all 471 human contestants and in the top three AI systems (https://ioai-official.org/ai-models-track/ioai%c2%b2-2026-re...).
We have a public bank for ML and Data at Leeroopedia (https://leeroopedia.com/): around 100k pages extracted by experimenting on papers and repos, about 6M requests a month, about 28% from AI agents.
If you are at a growing company with a complex data estate across multiple systems and functions, and your data and AI team is stretched, we would love to help!

articles.title: SSA from bytecode: imperative pearl
articles.summary:
Ufuk made a comment that he enjoyed my description of SSA from bytecode in
Aaron’s livestream with me.
While filming the livestream—an intro to ZJIT internals—I got a little
nervous that people would shy away from our 1900 line add_iseq_to_hir
function. This function is responsible for converting CRuby’s stack based
bytecode for the YARV virtual machine into a high-level SSA IR for ZJIT to
analyze and optimize.
It takes bytecode that looks roughly like this:

push 3
push 4
add


into SSA form, giving an SSA value to each stack slot, ish:

v0 = const 3
v1 = const 4
v2 = add v0, v1


While our function is 2000 lines long because it handles a lot of specific
opcodes and weird facts about those opcodes, the core of it is small. Here is
that core.
What if a stack, but virtual
The bytecode assumes that when it is run, it will be operating on a stack. This
means that every opcode has implicit stack inputs and implicit stack outputs.
push 3, for example, has empty stack inputs and one stack output. By
contrast, add has two stack inputs and one stack output. Some instructions
such as nop are empty on both counts. As far as I can tell, all instructions
have at most one output.
These counts are known when looking at the bytecode: we can reason statically
about how many inputs and outputs each opcode has. Some are variadic, such as
send (call), but they come bearing an argument count in a nearby field.
Let’s model how the first example runs on the VM by adding a view of the stack
after each instruction has run. The stack will be displayed as a list
left-to-right, where the left is the bottom and the right is the top.

       ; []
push 3 ; [3]
push 4 ; [3, 4]
add    ; [7]


Because the input counts and output counts are static, when ZJIT reads through
the bytecode, we can run the stack parts of it at compile-time.
We don’t really need to know what the values on the stack are; we only need
to keep track of where they came from. And when I say “where they came from”, I
mean that we name each instruction and refer to its output by the instruction’s
name. I like how the paper Design of the Java HotSpot™ Client Compiler for
Java 6 (PDF) puts it:
An instruction that loads or computes a value represents both the operation
and its result, so that operands can be represented as pointers to previous
instructions.
Here is what that looks like for the above example. In addition to the run-time
stack, I will also write the SSA instruction to indicate that we are generating
new code:

       ; []
push 3 ; v0 = const 3
       ; [v0]
push 4 ; v1 = const 4
       ; [v0, v1]
add    ; v2 = add v0, v1
       ; [v2]


This is neat! We have transformed stack based bytecode to a form where
instructions can directly reference their inputs. You may notice, though, that
v0 and v2 both end up in the same stack slot (the first element). This is
why I said earlier “giving an SSA value to each stack slot, ish”.
The difference between the two is time. v0 was in the operand stack at one
point but now v2 is. This is kind of why I describe SSA as “pushing time
through the IR”.
Alright, let’s implement it.
Implementation
We’ll start with the real (“concrete”) interpreter of the bytecode, which
operates on a value stack. This gives you a simplified version of how Ruby
internals work:

def interpret(bytecode)
  stack = []
  bytecode.each do |op|
    case op
    in [:push, c]
      stack << c
    in [:add]
      right = stack.pop
      left = stack.pop
      stack << left + right
    else
      raise "Unknown op #{op}"
    end
  end
  stack.pop
end

bytecode = [
  [:push, 3],
  [:push, 4],
  [:add],
]

puts interpret(bytecode)  # 7


Now let’s look at the abstract intepreter, which by contrast operates on an SSA
stack. You can see that they are quite similar looking:

def to_ssa(bytecode)
  code = []
  stack = []
  bytecode.each do |op|
    case op
    in [:push, c]
      name = :"v#{code.length}"
      code << "#{name} = const #{c}"
      stack << name
    in [:add]
      name = :"v#{code.length}"
      right = stack.pop
      left = stack.pop
      code << "#{name} = add #{left}, #{right}"
      stack << name
    else
      raise "Unknown op #{op}"
    end
  end
  code
end

bytecode = [
  [:push, 3],
  [:push, 4],
  [:add],
]

puts to_ssa(bytecode)
# v0 = const 3
# v1 = const 4
# v2 = add v0, v1


The names could be anything as long as they are unique. For simplicity and
ease of reading, I picked the length of the code array, which grows
monotonically. This is an array/vector-based analogue to the real-pointer
approach in the HotSpot paper from above.
Ta da! You have built a small abstract interpreter.
Now to make it global (to handle control flow) you need some kind of
inter-basic-block data flow mechanism such as phi nodes or basic block
parameters. Perhaps more on that in another post, but for now, you may enjoy
my collection of other people’s writing about that.
Conclusion
I originally wanted to title this blog post “you could have invented abstract
interpretation” or similar, but I decided that I find those titles obnoxious
because they assume the reader is or thinks of themself as unintelligent.
Perhaps we could have invented it.
The title is a bit of a tongue-in-cheek nod to the “functional pearl” papers
that I always felt should be simpler than they are but leave me confused. And
also kind of a nicer nod to SSA is Functional
Programming (PDF) by Andrew Appel.
References
A New Approach to Forth Native Code Generation (PDF, 1992)
Java Bytecode to Native Code Translation: The Caffeine Prototype and Preliminary Results (PDF, 1996) section 3.2
CACAO - A 64 bit JavaVM Just-in-Time Compiler (PDF, 1997) section 3
Fast, Effective Code Generation in a Just-In-Time Java Compiler (PDF, 1998) section 2.2, the mimic stack
The Jalapeño Dynamic Optimizing Compiler for Java™ (PDF, 1999)
Dynamic optimization through the use of automatic runtime specialization (1999) section 3.4

articles.title: Distributed Ray Tracer
articles.summary:
Hey HN, I'm Julius, I'm a backend engineer at Hatchet and created this demo to show off some of Hatchet's new features, primarily durable streams and serverless endpoints. Those, however, are just background details that made this significantly easier to scale. By distributing the rendering across many different nodes, orchestrated using Hatchet, it makes it possible to render quite high fidelity scenes fairly quickly. All of this would be possible on a single machine, but would be much slower without dedicated hardware (RT cores, etc).
The renderer itself is using well-known ray tracing techniques, with no special considerations there. The renderer is a slightly modified version of https://github.com/ekzhang/rpt, with additional support for SDF scripting using https://docs.rs/fidget/latest/fidget/.  SDFs have been popular in the demoscene community, though perhaps not super well known outside of that, and are capable of creating some fantastic looking scenes: https://www.shadertoy.com/view/ld3Gz2. The coolest part here is using a DSL to represent the SDFs in a rendering pipeline, and using LLMs with a chat interface to create them.
The source is available here: https://github.com/hatchet-dev/distributed-ray-tracer

if CEO and founder Jensen Huang is ousted, according to people
familiar with the matter.
Here’s Kress’s LinkedIn profile.
Semafor earlier confirmed that Nvidia’s board is preparing to
oust Huang as soon as Wednesday, after media reports detailed
that he had a second extramarital affair. The Nvidia board briefed
the White House on its planned meeting, according to a senior
administration official.
Nvidia has tapped an outside search firm to find the
company’s next CEO, Bloomberg reported. One person being
considered for the top job is Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji,
who was among the executives considered for Intel CEO in 2019,
according to another person familiar with the matter.
Kara Swisher spitballed Tim Cook as an idea, but that’s nonsense. If Cook wanted to be the CEO of a Fortune 2 company, he’d still be CEO at Apple. Apple despises Nvidia and Nvidia despises Apple. Cook may well be enjoying this fiasco, but only as entertainment drizzled with fresh farm-to-table schadenfreude — not as a personal opportunity.
Srouji, though, is an interesting name. Semafor doesn’t say whether this is just wishful thinking on the part of Nvidia’s board or if Srouji has indicated receptiveness. Srouji has been at Apple since 2008 but he’s a bit of a cipher. My spidey-sense can’t tell if he bleeds six colors or not.
Mark Gurman — and no one else — claimed last year that Srouji went to Tim Cook and threatened to leave for another company. Srouji called bullshit on this with a memo that stated flatly, “I love my job at Apple, and I don’t plan on leaving anytime soon.” Then, in April, when John Ternus was named Cook’s successor, Srouji was simultaneously promoted to the new position of Chief Hardware Officer.
So one scenario is that Srouji feels no allegiance to Apple, and Tim Cook and John Ternus are the sort of leaders who, when faced with a threat from a subordinate, give in because they’re cowards, and give a big promotion to someone who might leave Apple for a rival just weeks after Apple’s CEO transition.
Another scenario is that Srouji meant what he said, loves his job at Apple, and truly is John Ternus’s trusted and trustworthy hardware lieutenant. In this case, Nvidia’s board leaking that they’re considering Srouji to replace Huang is like someone in hell saying they’re considering ordering some ice water. My money is on this scenario.

Jenson Huang, in an on-stage interview with Garry Tan at Y Combinator’s “Startup School”, three months ago, on how Nvidia is organized (starting at 17m:00s):
Huang: You’re going to build an F1 racer, but you’re going to build it in
a way that you can drive. You should adapt the car to you.
Somebody asked me, Jensen, if you don’t use conventional
management techniques and organizational techniques, what’s going
to happen when you leave the company?
Well, when I die on the job — someday — I told them they’ll just
have to reshape the company for the next CEO. And the reason
that’s wisdom is because we’re the F1 drivers. We’re the racers.
And the world is really competitive, and we’ve got to win. We’ve
got to achieve our mission. And so whatever it takes to fit the
car to you, whatever it takes to fit the organization to you,
that’s what you got to do. And the next CEO, whatever their
personality is, they can figure it out.
Tan: Amazing.
It now seems like there are better words than “amazing” to describe this structure and strategy, for what was — at the time of the interview — the biggest company by market cap in the world. As of this morning, they’ve dropped to #2, and I think they’re going to drop to #3 or #4 soon.
By Huang’s own description, Nvidia needs to completely rebuild the car for his successor. And Huang left at least two huge turds in the cockpit of the existing car. (My money says there are more turds yet to be revealed.)

articles.title: Jensen Huang Was Banging an Nvidia Vice President Too
articles.summary:
Ryan Mac, Tripp Mickle, and Georgia Gee, reporting for The New York Times:
Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for
an affair with a woman who U.S. intelligence determined is a
Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an
executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked
at the company.
The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with
Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, said the
people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe
sensitive information. Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees
are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict”
including “personal relationships,” and the company states that it
“promptly investigates reports of misconduct.” Many corporations
have policies against managers having relationships with
subordinates.
Mr. Huang, 63, and Ms. Powell, 48, were captured on video being
affectionate at a San Jose, Calif., hotel during a Nvidia
conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at
the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.
Both Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell are married to other people.
If there are other affairs, it seems pretty likely that intelligence agencies know about those too. He wasn’t very secretive about either of the affairs that have come out so far. If there are more, those who know about them in the China-hawk U.S. national security community are going to keep leaking new ones every few days until Huang resigns or the Nvidia board fires him. And at this point I would bet there are more affairs.
When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship
with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, “I don’t think you should be
talking to me directly.” He then hung up. [...]
In March, Ms. Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer
conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using A.I. to aid in
breakthroughs in health care and biology. Her presentation used
cartoon depictions of Mr. Huang.
During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel
for meetings. Mr. Huang and Ms. Powell were seen being
affectionate at the hotel. One bystander captured the interaction
on their phone, three people briefed on the incident said. Mr.
Huang’s security workers witnessed the bystander with the phone
and sequestered the person, the people said. The workers then
asked the person to sign a nondisclosure agreement.
The Times doesn’t say whether the “bystander” signed the agreement, whether they were offered anything in exchange for signing it, or whether they were an Nvidia employee (in which case the offer could have been that they get to keep their job in exchange for signing it). The Times also doesn’t say whether Huang’s security team carries a pad of NDAs with them, like meter maids do with parking tickets.

articles.summary: Today's links Uber's labor crash: Replacing serfs with robots just doesn't pencil out. Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: Asimov inspired Al Qaeda; PATRIOT Act scares Canadian customers off US servers; EFF v Trump; Internet infrastructure is unsupported and failing; Nominative determinism debunked; How to fight Trump; Burglars v burglary; NYT said Hitler was only kidding; Folky Song Funny Note; Surviving autocracy; Corporate criminals. Uber's labor crash (permalink) There's a specific kind of lie that tech bosses tell: the "premature truth." That's a lie that they excuse by saying it'll come true soon: https://pluralistic.net/2024/12/04/its-not-a-lie/#its-a-premature-truth Elon Musk is the world's most enthusiastic teller of these lies. That's not surprising: any kind of radical promise about the automotive sector has a 90% chance of being this kind of bullshit. Musk can barely mention the subject of transportation without lying his face off: from "full self-driving" to "hyperloops" to "tunnels" to "flying cars," Musk is a fountain of extremely untrue "premature truths": https://karlbode.com/musks-fake-flying-car-and-ceo-said-a-thing-journalism/ But Musk has plenty of competition when it comes to lies about futuristic cars. Long before Musk switched on his first bullshit factory, Uber was spending billions to spray the world with lies about cars. Uber has always lied about everything, from driver pay to the company's finances. Now, lying about driver pay is relatively low-risk for a company like Uber. After all, the company created the app-based worker misclassification playbook, designed to make vulnerable and precarious workers even more vulnerable and precarious. The lies Uber tells about its workforce only have to survive contact with credulous municipal governments so that they keep up a supply of get-out-of-jail-free cards for Uber's many labor, licensing and consumer rights violations. But lying about your finances is another matter altogether. When Uber lies about its finances, it is lying to rich people, and (unlike workers), rich people have many ways to punish people who lie to them. Despite this, Uber spent more than a decade lying flagrantly and lavishly about its balance sheet. The most shameless financial lie Uber told is that it was profitable due to the increased valuation of the many ride-hailing companies around the world that Uber owns large shares in. How did Uber come to own large shares in these companies? It happened after Uber's competing ride-hailing companies in countries around the world failed. Uber's subsidiaries lost billions of dollars, and eventually Uber sold them to its (also money-losing) domestic rivals in all-stock deals that saw Uber acquiring vast amounts of worthless, illiquid shares in the world's failing ride-hailing companies. Then, for years, Uber would announce that its stake in these companies had appreciated in value. These revaluations were purely vibes-based. Uber's former rivals were privately held, and while small volumes of shares traded hands in private deals, Uber's pronouncements that, say, the Chinese company Didi was now worth vastly more than it had been worth a few months before was sheer fantasy dressed up as profits: https://pluralistic.net/2022/02/11/bezzlers-gonna-bezzle/#gryft Uber did this over and over (and over and over), relentlessly dogged by Hubert Horan, an aviation analyst who became the world's foremost close-reader of Uber's financial statements: https://pluralistic.net/2023/08/09/accounting-gimmicks/#unter Despite these lies, Uber eventually found a way for its early investors to cash out, through a very successful IPO that saw the House of Saud made whole (and then some) on the $31b they plowed into the business so that it could lose $0.41 on every dollar it brought in for the preceding 13 years. The most remarkable thing about Uber's IPO was the company's S1, the prospectus that tells normie investors how the company will eventually find its way to profit. That's where you'll find Uber's claim that its "total addressable market" is every journey made by taxi, private car, train and bus, for everyone in the world: https://stratechery.com/2019/uber-questions/ Despite the wild implausibility of this ambition, the company did achieve actual profitability after its IPO. It got there through the simple expedient of paying drivers less and charging riders more. The company spies on its drivers to calculate the lowest wage they'll accept, based on their inferred economic desperation, a process that Veena Dubal calls "algorithmic wage discrimination": https://pluralistic.net/2023/04/12/algorithmic-wage-discrimination/#fishers-of-men They also use surveillance data about riders to calculate the highest price you'll pay for a journey. Investors call this "personalized pricing," while everyone else calls it "surveillance pricing." It's a way for Uber to reach into your bank account and reduce the value of your dollars, by charging you more than the next person would pay for the same service: https://pluralistic.net/2025/06/24/price-discrimination/ This is something AI turns out to be extremely good at. Businesses can program chatbots to automatically segment their customers and employees based on surveillance data and then perform a series of automated experiments to find the highest prices and lowest wages they'll accept: https://pluralistic.net/2026/07/30/pay-for-privacy/#ab2654 When it comes to wage theft and price gouging, Uber leads the pack. They've really demonstrated just how much consumer and labor surplus can be diverted to capital with the aid of AI. Of course, it helps that they're willing to lie like crazy. Uber routinely claims that it pays its drivers hourly rates that are far in excess of minimum wage, but it helpfully omits that drivers only get paid while they have a passenger in the car, and that the company punishes drivers who turn down too many unprofitable jobs. Drivers only get paid for a fraction of the time they spend working for Uber, and on top of that, they have to pay for fuel, insurance, depreciation, loan interest, and the cost of getting vomit out of their back seats. Add it all up and Uber drivers make peanuts. In Toronto, Uber pay nets out to something like $2.50/hour: https://pluralistic.net/2024/02/29/geometry-hates-uber/#toronto-the-gullible $2.50/hour isn't a living wage anywhere in Canada, but it's especially terrible in Toronto, one of the world's most expensive cities. Uber can only be profitable for so long as drivers continue to subsidize its business, and so long as riders are willing to pay more than they ever did under the traditional taxi system (much of which was seen off by Uber's Saudi-subsidized decade of predatory pricing, which also induced a lost decade in global transit investment). Inflation (supercharged by AI pricing) has hit all workers, but it's been especially hard on Uber drivers, who didn't have any financial cushion to start with. Eventually, drivers were bound to turn their backs on Uber. "Eventually" is now, according to Uber's Q3 earnings call, where CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told investors that "driver supply [was] not keeping pace with strong consumer demand in several international markets": https://s23.q4cdn.com/407969754/files/doc_earnings/2026/q3/earnings-result/Uber-Q3-26-Earnings-Press-Release.pdf As The Gig Economy Project writes, the driver shortage is especially sharp in India and Brazil, two gigantic countries where (according to Uber CFO Balaji Krishnamurthy), there is too much consumer "price sensitivity": https://thegigeconomyproject.substack.com/p/has-uber-finally-pushed-its-workers Uber's also having trouble getting drivers to accept the rock-bottom wages they're offering for food delivery. Despite this, Krishnamurthy assured investors that the company's measures to "improve driver availability" wouldn't affect their bottom line. Instead, Krishnamurthy promised to raise prices on riders elsewhere, something he called "re-balancing incentives": That is part of the art that we’ve got and then there is a lot of algorithmic science that goes into, if you have a dollar, what is the maximum predicted return for that dollar and should I invest that dollar in a driver in Brazil or should I invest that dollar in a rider in India, for example. The algorithm can structurally make these choices based on training on billions of trips and allocate these investments in the way that humans just can’t. The Gig Economy Project goes on to say that "robotaxis will fundamentally alter the unit economics of taxis, but we are still some time away from the point where robotaxis are price competitive with human-driven vehicles." Boy is this an understatement. Remember, Uber is already paying drivers sub-minimum, sub-starvation wages, which drivers must spend to cover all the capital, depreciation, maintenance and insurance costs, along with (skyrocketing) fuel costs. I can't think of any way in which replacing starvation-wage drivers who provide their own cars with $200k robotaxis that the company must operate, maintain and insure will work out better for the company than the current situation. This is as good as it gets for Uber, in other words. Being able to tap an army of desperate workers who supply 99% of Uber's business's capital and variable costs out of their own pockets is vastly superior to operating a fleet of expensive robots that Uber has to purchase and service. Profitable "driverless" cars have been around the corner for more than 15 years now. Waymo claims to have delivered this through the brute force expedient of using the most expensive sensors and vast amounts of incredibly expensive cloud computing, but their balance sheet remains stubbornly opaque. We don't know how often a "driverless" Waymo is just a remote control car, being piloted by a low-wage worker in an overseas call center (there's a reason Indian technologists joke that AI stands for "Absent Indians"): https://pluralistic.net/2024/01/29/pay-no-attention/#to-the-little-man-behind-the-curtain We also don't know how often a Waymo is being overseen by a high-waged engineer. What we do know is that that when GM was forced to reveal this number, it turned out that they'd replaced a single, low-waged cab driver with 1.5 engineers, each of whom earned an order of magnitude more than the cabbie they'd displaced: https://garymarcus.substack.com/p/could-cruise-be-the-theranos-of-ai Uber's claims that they were profitable (based on accounting gimmicks) were lies, but they were also premature truths: the company did become profitable (though price-gouging and wage-theft). But there's a limit to how low you can push your workforce's wages, and even if the AI crash delivers a fresh cohort of desperate workers who subsidize Uber's operations for a few more years, they, too, will eventually find that they can't live on $2.50/hour. When that day comes, robo-taxis won't save the business model. Robots may cost less per hour than Uber drivers (though not by much), but owning a robot is always going to be more expensive than getting drivers to supply free cars to Uber. If Uber can't sustain profitability with that massive subsidy, it is going to hit a wall, and it won't be pretty. articles.title: NYC’s venture capitalists need to love themselves
articles.summary:
I really want a lot of venture capital investors to work on their self-esteem.
After a few decades of supporting and mentoring New York City’s tech community, I hope I’m credible when I say I care a lot about how it thrives. So one of the most disappointing—and frankly surprising—things I’ve seen lately is how many investors in the greatest city in the world have been lowering themselves, sucking up for approval from a cohort of Silicon Valley tycoons who hate our city, hate our values, and want us to fail.
I’m furious because there are so many good people and good ideas here that deserve to thrive, and aren’t getting the chance. Why would anyone sit by while outsiders put our community down, only to let those same outsiders profit off us when we succeed anyway?
In fairness, I’m not talking about all of our city’s investors. Some are content to keep their heads down and hope the worst of the West Coast doesn’t notice them. But imagine if our other civic institutions worked this way: the Knicks timidly stepping onto the court and standing back while opponents charge the rim, or the Liberty letting the other team fire off shots unchallenged. This is not the New York City I know. What real New Yorker, when faced with a taxi cab headed toward them in a crosswalk, would say, “Oh, sorry, I was going to be walking here, but you go right ahead and run me over, good sir!”

It’s pathetic, and it’s bad for business. Our city is watching, and our kids are too.
HQ Zero
I’ve been lucky enough to watch brilliant friends build innovative businesses here, having each other’s backs and catalyzing a community that lifted up the city we all love.
And then, over and over, we watched our lawmakers line up to give billions in handouts to West Coast tycoons who’d already won the game. Even when the community stopped those giveaways, the companies still hired just as many people here as they’d promised—because people want to work in New York City. Our tech community's own data shows that, while the Bay Area lost tech jobs over the last 5 years, we've grown by 23%. We never needed to bribe these guys in the first place. (Unsurprisingly, many of the same people who once demanded access to New York taxpayers’ pockets started trashing our city and its most vulnerable residents the moment the freebies dried up.)
The lesson is simple, for the public sector and private investors alike: we don’t need to buy the love of people who hate New York, or act as if we’re inferior and desperate to import an economy from elsewhere. We don’t do that shit here. We don’t need to be thirsty. We can invest in the people who already love this city enough to build the future here. We are, you may learn, second to none.
Fortunately, we’ve replaced the timid, backwards-looking leadership of the past with people who believe in our ability to lead, build, and invent a better future. It’s no surprise that New Yorkers are more optimistic than they’ve been in decades, or that we have the lowest crime in recorded history—nor that the people who hate our city are lying about all of it. The very same tycoons who felt entitled to taxpayer handouts now feel entitled to treat our investors as feeder funds for their own goals. There is no future in funneling deals to firms trying to undermine our entire civic ecosystem.
Building value, having values
I’m still committed to the radical social ethos that you should be able to build tech companies worth hundreds of millions of dollars, that founders and employees can get fabulously wealthy while workers are paid fairly, that investors earn a solid return, and that everybody pays an appropriate tax rate to the city that made it all possible. I don’t care if it makes me a radical to think those opportunities shouldn’t be hoarded by the same three or four predatory jerks who can’t stop trashing New York.
It’s no secret that the rise of authoritarianism and bald-faced bigotry among Silicon Valley investors has led them to demonize our city. What’s almost too much to bear is watching people I’ve respected in New York look the other way while those leaders embrace rank misogyny, blatant antisemitism, unapologetic Islamophobia, and profound racism—so virulent that the most powerful venture capital firm in the world hired a partner on the basis that he strangled an unarmed Black man to death. I’m grateful that many of you tell me privately that you object and still hold onto your moral compass, which makes it all the more heartbreaking to watch so many go silent publicly.
Where is your self-respect? Because I’ll be honest: they are laughing at you for debasing yourselves in front of them, and they enjoy shitting on the city you call home. You should do work you’re proud of, that you feel good telling your family about, and that you’re excited to share with your community.
You should also do the math. A tiny handful of firms control the vast majority of late-stage funds, and you are not going to differentiate yourself by being a mindless feeder fund for the same 10 cancer capital firms as everyone else. If your only edge is competing on who can kiss Andreessen’s ass the most, you’re already fucked, kids. Look at how they already have to tap-dance—calling things “super intelligence” instead of “artificial intelligence” just to prove their fealty. How long until you’re asked to publicly rename your work, or tell a big lie about your city, just to stay in the room?
I’ve heard too many people in this town claim they don’t have any power, that their only job is returning capital to LPs. All you have to do is the simplest thing in the world: refuse to play along.
By contrast, if you bet on this wonderful community, connect to the next generation of innovators, and fight for the future instead of against it, there is limitless opportunity here. If you have to put it in a way your LPs can understand, explain that there is huge alpha in going the way that a16z is not. Call it “Anti-authoritarian Dynamism”. Explain that you’re going to strangle their deal flow, since founders of color and next-gen innovators don’t want to talk to the firms who hate New York City and hire killers. Tell them you’re choking off the supply chain of capital to the office where Daniel Penny works.
Side with the founders, not the funders
Just in case you don’t already know: Zohran Mamdani is your best friend. He wants the city to win, and our businesses to thrive. And those West Coast VCs who act deranged when you mention his name? They want your city destroyed, and when it's not, they lie and say that it already has been destroyed. Pick the side of your neighbors and your community, and speak up for the founders and entrepreneurs building the opportunities you want to be part of.
Just as importantly, speak up for yourself. It’s not viable in the long term for every outcome—and the small number of possible exits for your portfolio—to be controlled by the same handful of gatekeepers. I used to love helping friends turn cool new products into companies that provided good jobs; now that’s virtually impossible because the scale has gotten so absurd, and so few players decide who gets to participate. When I talk to people who are still early in their tech careers, the only names they know in the investor world are the usual suspects — not yours. They’ve never heard of your firms, of many of New York's most thoughtful and interesting and supportive investors, and they’re downright skeptical when I tell them to work with NYC-based investors instead of making a trip to Sand Hill Road. That all changes the moment New York’s tech leaders put their power behind an alternative narrative.
Simply saying “we are here, we exist, and we are not a satellite of the same tired agenda you’ve been hearing from Silicon Valley for years” would be hugely valuable for the entire New York City tech ecosystem. It's going to be especially resonant after the entire country just picked a political path that looks a lot like New York City's values — and is based on rejecting Big Tech's values. It would also, I expect, do wonders for your soul after years of enduring the quiet indignities of watching some horrid people chip away at your self-esteem.
Now, I know most of you aren’t inclined to go to war. That’s fine — you can still be nice. Jalen Brunson is really nice! Karl-Anthony Towns is really nice! Sabrina Ionescu is nice! But they really like to win, and they don’t take shit from anyone. You have to decide if you want to win, or if you want to get bullied on the playground by the people who actually have their heads in the game.
As a repeat founder who spends my time with makers — both the next generation of creators, and the people who’ve built great companies before them — I know where my loyalty lies. Those of us who build things know who we are. Those of us who love New York City are having one of the great moments of the modern era.
Do you know who you are? Are you going to join us?

articles.title: And Every New Boy That You Meet / He Doesn’t Know the Real Surprise
articles.summary:
Lingling Wei, reporting for The Wall Street Journal:
Before the affair that threatened his job as Nvidia’s chief
executive, Jensen Huang was introduced to his future romantic
interest, Alice Huang, by a Chinese businessman he’d known for a
decade, Kang Wei.
Kang also happened to be Alice Huang’s husband, said people who
know the couple.
For two years, Kang appeared to accept his wife’s romantic
relationship with the Nvidia CEO and spoke openly of their
closeness, these people said. Sometimes, Kang told associates,
half-jokingly, that she was a personal assistant to Jensen Huang,
they said.
The Cars’ “My Best Friend’s Girl” is not a bad song to have stuck in your head. Not a bad song at all.
Over the past decade, Kang and Alice Huang hopscotched from one
lucrative opportunity to the next — videogame companies,
pharmaceutical takeovers and cloud computing — each time weaving
a web of related entities, transferring stakes among themselves
and capitalizing on whatever connections were at hand, said people
familiar with the couple’s business dealings. Nvidia’s AI chips
were the latest play for a couple with a track record of riding
hot trades and, on occasion, running afoul of regulators.
Now the couple are the subject of a raft of investigations, and
the blast radius of their relations with Jensen Huang is
expanding.
U.S. officials believe that China’s intelligence services
recruited Alice Huang as an asset because of her access to the
chip-designer chief.
That sentence at the end clarifies what I think is, at the moment, a widely held misconception. The allegation that Alice Huang was a “spy” for Chinese intelligence isn’t she was a trained secret agent whose mission was to seduce Jensen Huang and infiltrate Nvidia. It’s that once the Chinese spooks learned of the affair — which, in hindsight, wasn’t well hidden — they gave Alice Huang an offer she couldn’t refuse. To do what, we don’t know, but it sure sounds like a part of it was to procure and smuggle Nvidia hardware in contravention of U.S. national security regulations.
